How to Run Product Competitive Analysis That Leads to Better Product Decisions
Lena HofmannLena Hofmann|Jul 13, 2026, 06:13 PM|13 min read
How to Run Product Competitive Analysis That Leads to Better Product Decisions
Share to
TL;DR: skill agent workflow for faster competitive research
Start your product competitive analysis as a decision system, not a note pile. This guide is for product managers, founders, marketers, researchers, and strategy teams who need a repeatable way to set scope, pick the right competitors, compare features, gather proof, normalize findings in a competitor feature matrix, and turn insights into owners, timelines, and KPIs.
Competitive research often breaks down when evidence lives in scattered tabs, docs, and meeting notes. That slows decisions and makes follow-through weak. A workspace like TicNote Cloud helps teams capture source evidence, organize competitor findings, and keep outputs shareable without losing context.
The result is a lightweight workflow: define the question, choose the analysis set, collect evidence, score what matters, and turn gaps into prioritized actions. Instead of ending with observations, you leave with a clear next move.
How to run product competitive analysis without getting lost in data
A strong product competitive analysis starts with a decision, not a spreadsheet. If you define the decision, scope, and audience first, you collect less noise and find more signal. That's also what makes the work usable later, whether you're updating a roadmap, reviewing pricing, or refining positioning.
Set the decision and timeframe first
Start with one live question. For example:
 Which feature should we prioritize this quarter?
 Should we change packaging or pricing?
 Where does onboarding fall behind competitors?
 Is our positioning still clear in the market?
This keeps the analysis tied to action. Without a decision, teams drift into endless collection. Define three things up front: the product area, the review period, and the depth required. A two-week onboarding review needs a different level of detail than a 12-month platform comparison.
Narrow the market slice
Don't study the whole category. Focus on the market slice your buyer actually sees. Narrow by:
 User segment
 Use case
 Geography
 Buying context
That prevents false comparisons. In many cases, your real alternatives are not just direct vendors. They may be spreadsheets, internal tools, agencies, or doing nothing at all. A useful competitor product analysis compares the options customers actually weigh.
Match outputs to stakeholder needs
Different teams need different views of the same facts:
 Product needs feature gaps, trade-offs, and priority signals
 Marketing needs positioning, claims, and messaging shifts
 Sales needs objection handling and deal-level comparisons
 Design needs workflow patterns and UX benchmarks
 Leadership needs market risk, timing, and strategic impact
Use one source of truth, then create tailored summaries from it. If you need a repeatable structure, this competitive analysis framework helps turn raw findings into strategy. The best competitive product analysis is proactive, refreshed on a regular cadence, and used to challenge stale assumptions before a rival launch forces a reaction.
Try TicNote Cloud for Free to keep competitor evidence, notes, and summaries in one searchable place.
Which competitors belong in your analysis set?
A strong product competitive analysis starts with the buyer's point of view, not your org chart. Customers don't sort options by software category. They compare anything that solves the same job, saves the same time, or replaces the same workflow. That's why your analysis set should include direct competitors, indirect competitors, and substitutes.
Split the market into three competitor types
Use this simple structure:
 Direct competitors: similar product, similar buyer, similar use case
 Indirect competitors: related product solving an adjacent problem
 Substitutes: manual workflows, spreadsheets, docs, email, or internal tools
For example, a meeting workspace may compete directly with transcription tools, indirectly with docs platforms, and as a substitute against a team's manual notes process. In practice, the user may compare all three in the same buying journey.
Build the list from customer language
The best inputs usually come from places where people explain trade-offs in plain words:
 user interviews
 support tickets
 win-loss notes
 search queries
 review sites and app stores
 Reddit threads and communities
 sales calls and demos
These sources show how buyers frame the problem. If prospects keep saying, "We also looked at Otter, Notion, and just using Google Docs," all three belong in your competitor product analysis.
Prioritize only 5 to 7 products
Don't track 20 companies at once. Use a short filter and keep the active set tight:
 market relevance
 overlap in core workflow
 threat level
 frequency of mention
A practical SaaS shortlist might include three direct rivals, two indirect tools, and one or two substitutes. If your category is still emerging, add one benchmark from an adjacent market. That gives you a clearer competitor feature comparison without drowning in noise. If you need a repeatable way to document each player, this guide to building useful competitor profiles can help.
Build a competitor feature comparison that reveals real gaps
A strong product competitive analysis does more than list features. It uses the right comparison framework for the decision in front of you, scores what users actually care about, and turns messy notes into a matrix your team can act on. The goal is not false precision. The goal is pattern recognition that leads to better product choices.
Pick the framework that fits the decision
Use different tools for different questions:
 SWOT analysis works best when you need a broad view of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.
 A positioning map helps you spot whitespace in the market and see how brands frame themselves.
 A competitor feature matrix is best for side-by-side product comparison when roadmap or packaging decisions are on the line.
If you're deciding whether to build, improve, bundle, or ignore a capability, the matrix is usually the clearest option.
Create a weighted comparison template
Your competitor feature comparison template should include:
 comparison categories
 scoring definitions
 weights by importance
 evidence links or source notes
 confidence level
 notes on what matters most to the target user
This keeps teams from overvaluing flashy features while missing onboarding friction, weak support, or low trust. A simple weighted model works well: score each item from 1 to 5, then multiply by its weight. For example, onboarding might be worth 20%, core workflow 30%, pricing and paywalls 15%, integrations 15%, UX clarity 10%, and trust signals 10%.
Score the full user experience, not just features
A useful competitor product analysis compares more than checkboxes. Score each competitor on:
 core features
 pricing model and packaging
 paywalls and trial limits
 time to value
 integrations
 UX clarity
 performance signals
 support depth
 positioning claims
Keep the scoring plain. A 1 to 5 or 1 to 10 scale is enough if every score has a short evidence note.
Normalize the data into a clean matrix
Raw observations vary. One product says "AI-powered." Another hides limits behind a paywall. Normalize that input into separate rows for:
 must-have features
 differentiators
 weak spots
A SaaS example might compare three note-taking tools. Tool A has rich recording but weak exports. Tool B has lower pricing but slow setup. TicNote Cloud stands out when teams need editable transcripts, cited AI outputs, project memory, and one-click reports in one place. Inside a Project, you can store transcripts, competitor notes, and decision logs together so the evidence stays attached to the conclusions.
Here is a simple text-based competitor feature matrix format:
 Recording: A 5 | B 4 | TicNote Cloud 5
 Editable transcripts: A 2 | B 1 | TicNote Cloud 5
 Integrations: A 4 | B 3 | TicNote Cloud 4
 Time to value: A 3 | B 2 | TicNote Cloud 4
 Report generation: A 2 | B 2 | TicNote Cloud 5
If you want a reusable structure, start with this competitive analysis template and scoring workflow and adapt the weights to your market. Then prompt your workspace: "Create a competitor feature matrix from these notes, group rows by must-haves, differentiators, and weaknesses, and show weighted scores with evidence." That gives you a competitive product analysis that is consistent, transparent, and decision-ready.
Where should you collect evidence for a competitive product analysis?
A strong product competitive analysis starts with evidence from four places: official company materials, hands-on testing, third-party sources, and customer language. When you combine all four, you get a clearer view of what a competitor says, what the product actually does, how the market reacts, and why users switch, stay, or complain.
Review official sources first
Start with assets the company controls. These pages reveal positioning, pricing logic, product maturity, and strategic direction:
 Website homepage and product pages
 Pricing pages and plan limits
 Help docs and knowledge bases
 Release notes or changelogs
 Webinars, product tours, and demo videos
 Job posts and hiring pages
A pricing page shows monetization. Help docs show complexity. Changelogs show shipping speed. Job posts often reveal strategic bets, such as enterprise expansion, AI investment, or new integrations.
Test the product yourself
Next, run a hands-on competitor product analysis. Sign up for the free plan, request a demo, or walk through the trial and onboarding flow. This is where you spot time to value, hidden setup friction, and the activation moment (the point where the product first delivers value).
Track what happens in the first 5, 10, and 30 minutes. Note what is easy, what feels clunky, and what is blocked behind sales calls or upgrades.
Use third-party signals to balance the story
Official pages never tell the full story. Add external evidence from:
 G2 and Capterra reviews
 Reddit and niche communities
 App store reviews
 Search engine results pages
 Ad libraries and paid search copy
 Analyst pages or market overviews
These sources show the gap between brand messaging and customer perception. They also help validate a competitor feature comparison with patterns, not just claims.
Capture emotional drivers, not just features
The best competitive product analysis tracks repeated words and phrases. Watch for terms like "simple," "expensive," "enterprise-ready," "hard to set up," or "clunky." Also log why customers switch, why they stay, and what keeps coming up in complaints.
For every finding, save the source link, timestamp, and a short note so each claim stays verifiable. TicNote Cloud is useful here because teams can store review excerpts, transcripts, call notes, uploaded docs, and AI summaries in one Project, which makes it easier to defend a score later or refresh the analysis without starting over.
How do you turn competitor product analysis into roadmap decisions?
A product competitive analysis only matters when it changes what your team does next. The goal is not to collect more notes. It's to turn evidence into clear bets, owners, and measures of success. If you need a format for sharing decisions, this guide on turning research into action plans can help.
Find patterns, not isolated feature gaps
Start with clusters, not single requests. If three competitors reduce friction in onboarding, explain pricing better, and show stronger trust signals, that pattern matters more than one missing feature on your roadmap.
Look for repeated themes such as:
 onboarding drop-off points
 weak packaging or confusing pricing
 missing trust elements like proof, security, or case studies
 UX friction in core flows
 unmet jobs to be done (the real task users hire the product to solve)
Then separate table stakes from differentiators:
 Table stakes are features buyers expect to see.
 Differentiators create a reason to switch or buy.
 Overbuilding is a risk when a competitor feature adds complexity but little customer value.
Assign owners, timelines, and measurable KPIs
Every insight should become one action. That action needs four fields:
 accountable owner
 due date
 dependency note
 KPI
Useful KPIs include activation rate, win rate, feature adoption, demo conversion, or lower objection frequency. This turns competitor product analysis into operating work, not a slide deck that dies after the meeting.
Align teams around trade-offs
Different teams own different responses:
 Product owns feature, UX, or packaging changes.
 Marketing sharpens positioning and proof.
 Sales updates battlecards and objection handling.
 Leadership decides which trade-offs fit strategy.
Present findings as options with evidence, confidence, and likely impact. Don't drop a long research dump on the room. A strong competitor feature comparison becomes valuable only when it changes roadmap priorities, messaging, or go-to-market choices in a measurable way.
How to generate a competitive research report and matrix step by step
This workflow uses TicNote Cloud as the example, but the process works for any team that needs a repeatable product competitive analysis system. The goal is simple: collect public evidence, keep it organized in one place, and turn it into a report your team can review, edit, and use in roadmap discussions.
Start with one project for one market
On the Web platform, begin by creating a Project for the market, segment, or product line you want to study. Keeping one analysis inside one project matters because research compounds over time. New files, notes, and outputs stay connected instead of getting buried across docs and chat threads.

Define the analysis scope clearly
Next, enter the niche or industry, your target location, and five to ten competitor names or URLs. That gives the system a clean comparison set and reduces noisy results.
You can also narrow the brief with a focus area, such as:
 pricing
 customer reviews
 social media presence
 product range
That one choice keeps the competitor product analysis tied to the decision you actually need to make.
Review the outputs and turn them into briefs
After processing, the agent returns a structured report and a visual HTML competitor feature matrix. The written file typically includes an executive summary, comparison table, competitor profiles, market gaps, and recommended actions.
Open the report to check claims, refine wording, and align the conclusions with your team's priorities. Because the content is editable, you're not stuck with static exports. Cited AI outputs also make verification easier when someone asks, "Where did this come from?"
Then review the visual matrix for faster discussion in meetings.
This is where teams can turn findings into a shareable brief for leadership, product, or marketing. A strong product competitive analysis works best when it becomes a team habit, not a one-time deck. Start with the decision you need to make. FAQ
What is the difference between product competitive analysis and market research?
Market research looks at the big picture: customer segments, demand, trends, and category shifts. Product competitive analysis is narrower and more practical. It compares real alternatives against your product, including feature depth, user experience, positioning, pricing trade-offs, and why buyers may switch.
How often should you update a product competitive analysis?
Use a light refresh every month or quarter to track visible changes. Then run a deeper review before a launch, pricing update, repositioning effort, or market expansion. That rhythm helps teams catch meaningful moves without turning competitor product analysis into a full-time job.
What should a competitor feature comparison template include?
A useful competitor feature comparison template should include competitor names, target segment, core features, pricing and packaging, onboarding notes, integrations, UX observations, positioning, evidence links, weighted scores, and recommended actions. What is competitive analysis? How to do one (+ template)
Author:Alex Lindley
14 min read
May 21, 2026
Contributors:Faizan Ali and Cecilia Meis
A competitive analysis tells you how rivals attract, convince, and keep the customers you're trying to win — but the surfaces where that competition plays out have expanded.
Prospects are forming opinions about your brand inside AI search platforms before they ever visit your site. Standard competitive analyses miss this. They cover competitors' websites, marketing, and reputation, but stop short of AI visibility, which increasingly drives buyer decisions.
In this article, you’ll learn what competitive analysis is, how to run one across all three surfaces of a competitor's brand, and how to spot where competitors are winning in AI search. You'll also get a free template to organize your findings.
What is competitive analysis?
Competitive analysis is the process of researching and documenting competitors’ business strategies (like their product, marketing, and sales strategies) so you can use those insights to sharpen your own approach. It's also called competition analysis or competitive market analysis.
In 2026, a complete competitive analysis covers three surfaces:
 What the brand says about itself through its site’s marketing and sales content
 What third parties say about the brand through user reviews, press coverage, and community discussions
 What AI search platforms say about the brand, including if and how often it’s mentioned, the sentiment of those mentions, and which prompts it shows up in
The first two surfaces are familiar territory. The third is newer, and it shapes which brands prospects consider before they ever reach a website.
Types of competitors
To get the most valuable insights from competitive analysis, you need to identify and analyze the right competitors.
There are three types of competitors: direct, indirect, and aspirational. Each plays a different role in your strategy, and shows up differently across the three surfaces of competitor analysis.
Direct competitors
Direct competitors target similar audiences and offer similar products or services. Analyzing them should be your top priority because they’re the easiest to learn from and compare against.
Say you run a food delivery app targeting urban professionals. DoorDash is a direct competitor because it delivers restaurant meals to the same audience.
Indirect competitors
Indirect competitors offer different products or services but solve the same core need. They're worth analyzing after direct competitors, as changes in their strategies often signal broader market shifts that affect demand.
For a food delivery app, meal kit services like HelloFresh are indirect competitors — they reach busy people who want home-cooked meals, but with ingredient kits rather than restaurant meals delivered ready to eat.
Aspirational competitors
Aspirational competitors are industry leaders you admire and model your strategy after, even if you're not competing for the same customers. Study them when you're planning to grow beyond your current business model.
For a food delivery app, Uber is an aspirational competitor. It targets a similar audience and offers a similar service, but its platform also includes ride-hailing and package delivery. These are services the app could add as it scales.
Benefits of competitor analysis
The benefits of competitor analysis include:
 Benchmarking your performance: Comparing your traffic, rankings, conversions, and brand presence against direct rivals shows you where you stand and where you're falling behind
 Learning from others’ successes and failures: Studying what worked and didn't work for competitors accelerates your own path forward
 Identifying AI visibility gaps: Knowing where competitors appear (and don't appear) in AI-generated answers shows you which on- and off-site signals to strengthen
 Discovering untapped opportunities: Identifying market gaps reveals where competitors are overlooking customer segments, marketing channels, or key features
 Sharpening your positioning: Understanding how competitors describe themselves and their products helps you differentiate your brand more clearly to your target audience
How to do a competitive analysis
A competitive analysis is a multi-step process that covers your competitors' websites, third-party coverage, and AI visibility.
By the end, you’ll have a clear picture of how your competitors operate, and where your brand fits in.
1. Copy our competitive analysis template
Make a copy of our free competitive analysis template to organize your findings as you work through the steps below.
2. Identify competitors
Identify competitors using a combination of research methods, since no single method gives you a complete view of who you’re up against.
Find competitors by:
 Searching for your product and service types in Google and looking at the top-ranking results
 Asking AI search platforms for a list of businesses with similar products or services
 Testing related prompts to see which brands are mentioned or recommended
 Checking third-party content like reviews, listicles, and comparison articles to see which brands buyers research alongside you
 Asking your sales team about other solutions that prospects tend to consider
 Surveying former customers to identify which competitors they switched to
 Reviewing the competitive domains the Semrush Market Overview tool lists in your “Market Players” report
 Viewing the “Competitors” report in the Organic Rankings for your domain
Once you’ve listed competitors, sort them by type: direct, indirect, and aspirational. Then, select three direct competitors to analyze. This way, you’ll gather a range of high-impact insights without getting overwhelmed.
You can add more competitors later, including indirect and aspirational ones, as you extend your analysis.
3. Analyze competing products and services
Analyze competing products and services to better position and price your offerings to meet customer needs.
Start with value propositions. Study your competitors' marketing content to understand what problems they solve, how they solve them, and who they help. Compare these value propositions against yours to better differentiate your offerings.
Next, study your competitors’ product or service information to understand:
 Core features and capabilities: The main functionalities and unique features your competitors offer. Explore how these features meet (and don’t meet) customer needs, so you can capitalize on market gaps.
 Pricing: Review your competitors’ pricing to identify whether they target premium, mid-range, or budget segments. Use this to evaluate the competitiveness of your pricing, especially if you target the same segment.
Record your findings in your competitive analysis report.
4. Uncover competitors’ marketing channels and content formats
Uncovering what marketing channels and content formats drive the most traffic to competing sites provides valuable insights for your own marketing strategy.
Check competitors’ top traffic sources with a competitive analysis tool like Semrush’s Traffic & Market Toolkit. Enter a competitor’s domain and click “Analyze.”
Scroll to the “Traffic Channel Distribution” section to view the top traffic sources for the competitor’s domain.
Next, go to the toolkit’s Top Pages tool to see which channels drive the most traffic to individual pages. Click any page to see its entrance sources.
Study these traffic sources to gain insights. For example, a high portion of referral traffic may indicate the competitor has partnerships with industry influencers or has been featured on popular sites in your niche.
Next, review your competitors’ social media presence, including which platforms they use, the content formats they use, and engagement levels.
Evaluate the other types of content your competitors create as well: blog posts, email newsletters, webinars, or online courses. For example, if competitors have a blog, what kind of content do they publish, and how frequently?
Use a tool like AI Traffic to learn which AI search platforms send your competitors the most traffic.
Higher AI referral traffic often indicates stronger visibility signals across a competitor’s site, brand reputation, and third-party coverage.
5. Research your competitors’ sales processes
Research your competitors' sales processes to understand how they connect with prospects throughout the buying journey.
The sales process typically involves four stages:
 Presenting the offering: Understand how competitors communicate value and demonstrate their solutions to prospects. For instance, businesses that sell big-ticket items may have dedicated sales teams that work closely with prospects.
 Following up: Study how competitors stay in touch with prospects. Tactics include sending automated email reminders and making phone check-ins.
 Closing: Look at how competitors convert interested prospects. They might offer discounts, money-back guarantees, or product bundles to encourage purchases.
 Retention: Consider how competitors encourage customers to make repeat purchases or stay subscribed to their services. Perhaps they offer a loyalty scheme or exclusive customer content.
Start by engaging with your competitors’ marketing materials: subscribe to their newsletters, request demos, and attend their webinars. As you do this, observe how they communicate, follow up, and guide prospects through each stage.
Pay attention to their messaging style, contact frequency, and the tools or offers they use to build trust and move leads toward a purchase. The messaging competitors use throughout their sales process reinforces the brand associations AI platforms pick up across their site and third-party coverage.
6. Study customer feedback and ratings
Studying competitors' customer feedback and ratings reveals opportunities to win business from their customers and others like them.
These same signals also shape AI visibility: AI search platforms retrieve signals from user reviews, forum mentions, and third-party coverage when deciding which brands to mention and recommend.
Public sources of customer feedback and ratings include:
 Review aggregator platforms like G2 and Trustpilot. See what customers praise competitors for and what they’re unhappy about. Pay attention to recurring themes — if multiple customers complain about the same issue, it’s likely a significant weakness you could capitalize on.
 Social media platforms like X (formerly Twitter), Reddit, and LinkedIn. What prospects and customers say about competitors on these platforms can reveal where they shine or fall short. Use tools like Mention or Brand Monitoring to track social mentions.
 News publications: Check reputable news outlets for mentions of your competitors, and evaluate both the positive and negative comments. The Brand Monitoring tool can help with this.
Once you've gathered the feedback, use it to refine your positioning around competitor gaps and strengthen your off-site presence by encouraging satisfied customers to leave reviews.
AI search platforms weigh review quality and consistency when forming brand associations, so a strong review presence pays off in AI visibility too.
Document your findings in your competitive analysis report.
7. Assess AI visibility
Assess competitors’ AI visibility to learn how AI search platforms mention and cite them.
Start by launching the Semrush AI Visibility Toolkit, entering a competitor’s domain, and clicking “Check AI Visibility.”
The tool will display the competitor’s overall AI visibility (as a score out of 100) and the volumes of mentions and citations — both overall and across various AI search platforms.
Compare this against your own domain to see where you stand.
Next, switch to the Narrative Drivers tool to see your competitor’s share of voice, which reveals how often it appears in non-branded prompts.
You'll also see sentiment trends, the topics AI platforms most often associate with the brand, and the top domains driving AI citations for non-branded prompts in your category.
Prioritize building your brand presence across these domains to improve your AI visibility.
Use the Competitor Research tool to compare your AI visibility against your competitors' side by side.
Enter your domain alongside up to four competitor domains, then click "Run competitor analysis" to see where rivals get cited and your brand doesn't.
Navigate to the “Topics & Prompts” report, click “Prompts” to view prompts, and then click “Missing.”
Note the prompts you want AI search platforms to feature you on. Then, set up the Prompt Tracking tool to monitor their performance in ChatGPT, Gemini, and Google AI Mode.
Repeat the tracking setup for your competitor’s domain. Then, record all findings in your competitive analysis report.
8. Establish competitors’ strengths and weaknesses
Establish competitors’ strengths and weaknesses based on the detailed information you’ve gathered, so you can evaluate where you stand against them.
A competitor's strengths might include strong product-market fit, effective marketing campaigns, or consistent positive sentiment across reviews and AI answers. Weaknesses might include limited AI visibility, gaps in customer support, or pricing that's misaligned with their market segment.
Document your findings in your competitive analysis report.
9. Determine your positioning
Determining your positioning translates everything you've learned about your competitors into a clear angle for your own brand.
Conduct an analysis of your business’s strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT). Then, define the unique value you offer.
Maybe it’s a feature that solves a pain point more effectively, a superior onboarding experience, or a more flexible pricing structure. These differentiators form the core of your unique value proposition.
Also consider the customer segments you'll target. If you've identified a customer segment your competitors have overlooked, focus your product development and marketing efforts on serving their needs.
Once you've mapped your positioning, consider how it translates to AI search. The attributes AI platforms associate with your competitors, such as their pricing, reliability, and use case fit, are shaped by the same signals you've analyzed throughout this process.
Your positioning should account not just for how you differentiate on your website, but also for how you want AI systems to describe and recommend you.
Record everything in your competitor analysis report.
Competitive analysis example (step by step)
I ran a basic competitive analysis for a fictional coffee subscription service to give you an idea of how the process works and the insights you can get.
Let’s go through this competitive analysis example, step by step:
Competitor analysis
First, identify competitors by Googling relevant keywords like “coffee subscription” and noting which sites appeared near the top.
I also looked at coffee-related roundups and reviews, like the Bon Appétit roundup below.
Next, I used Semrush’s Market Overview tool to find more competitors. Since I didn’t have a domain for my fictional coffee subscription service, I used a competitor’s domain instead.
I also ran the same competitor domain through the Organic Rankings tool to see if additional competitors surfaced.
After confirming that these competitors offered coffee subscriptions, I sorted them into direct, indirect, or aspirational competitors.
I then chose three direct competitors to analyze: Bean Box, Trade Coffee, and Atlas Coffee Club.
Product strategy analysis
Next, I analyzed my competitors’ product strategies by reviewing their landing pages, frequently asked questions pages, and checkout flows.
I noticed all three competitors offer gift subscriptions, which signals demand and tells me I should offer them too.
Marketing strategy analysis
Analyzing my competitors’ marketing strategies with the Traffic & Market Toolkit, I learned my competitors get significant direct traffic — but this is likely driven by existing customers.
Organic search was a key channel (especially for Bean Box), while AI traffic was a largely untapped traffic source. So, I could use SEO to attract leads from search engines and AI search platforms. Referrals, email marketing, and paid search could also be good traffic sources.
I reviewed my competitors’ social media accounts and recorded key insights in my competitive analysis report.
The analysis pointed to a few moves:
 Pursue Instagram marketing with influencer partnerships, since competitors favor this approach
 Focus video content on TikTok rather than YouTube — competitors post frequently on TikTok but haven't published YouTube videos in years
 Skip Facebook and X, where competitors have stopped posting regularly. Threads is a better option for short-form text content, given Trade Coffee's consistent activity there.
Finally, I analyzed my competitors’ onsite content.
Bean Box attracts substantial blog traffic even though it hasn’t published new content since 2022. There’s a good opportunity to attract visitors with fresh, high-quality content.
Sales strategy analysis
I analyzed my competitors’ sales strategies by exploring their product landing pages, checkout flows, and email newsletters.
All competitors use a quick quiz to help prospects choose the right coffee subscription. The quiz’s interactive nature gets prospects invested in the outcome, so they’re more likely to convert.
For example, here’s part of Atlas Coffee Club’s quiz:
All three brands also use special offers to encourage conversions, especially for long-term subscriptions and bulk purchases. Most of these offers go out through email newsletters, which helps them convert leads and re-engage churned customers.
Feedback analysis
For feedback analysis, I searched for “[competitor] reviews” on Google and reviewed relevant results on third-party review sites, industry blogs, and online communities.
When I could copy reviews in bulk, I pasted them into ChatGPT and asked it to summarize recurring themes, so I didn’t have to analyze the reviews manually.
I paid attention to recurring praises and complaints. Common praises indicate features that drive customer satisfaction, while frequent complaints reveal opportunities to outperform competitors by addressing unsolved gaps or frustrations.
AI visibility analysis
I then conducted an AI visibility analysis by running my competitors’ domains through Semrush’s AI Visibility Toolkit.
According to the Visibility Overview tool, all three competitors have relatively low AI visibility, with the bulk of their AI mentions coming from Google’s AI Overviews. So, investing in agentic search optimization (ASO) could be an impactful way to increase brand awareness and sales.
Next, I used the Narrative Drivers tool to check my competitors’ shares of voice:
Narrative Drivers also informed me that the top domains by citations for the coffee subscription service industry are reddit.com, en.wikipedia.org, tastingtable.com, and bonappetit.com.
Getting a Wikipedia page would likely be challenging in the short term. So, to improve my coffee subscription service’s AI visibility, I’d focus on building a Reddit presence and getting featured in Tasting Table’s and Bon Appétit’s product reviews and “best of” listicles.
Since I don’t have a domain to run through Competitor Research, I used Visibility Overview to research prompts featuring my competitors.
A few prompts, like “Coffee Collection and Cafés” and “How can I order coffee online easily,” featured multiple competitors.
Appearing in AI-generated answers for these prompts is a priority, so I set up the Prompt Tracking tool to monitor them across my competitors’ domains. I’ll do the same for my domain when it’s ready.
Determining my positioning
Finally, I determined my positioning by reviewing my findings on each competitor and conducting a SWOT analysis for my brand.
Where competitors excel, I looked for ways to match or exceed those strengths, such as building appeal with Gen Z consumers, a segment in which competitors already have a foothold.
Where competitors were weak, I looked to fill the gaps. The most obvious one: AI visibility.
Prioritizing ASO gives my brand a chance to win AI mentions and recommendations while competitors remain under-invested.
Create your competitive analysis report
A modern competitive analysis should capture how each rival shows up across all three surfaces: their site, third-party coverage, and AI visibility.
If you haven’t already, make a copy of our competitive market analysis template to organize your findings and turn them into an actionable strategy.
Keep these tips in mind as you fill it out:
 Base decisions on data: Let real data — not assumptions or guesses — guide your conclusions to make more impactful decisions
 Keep your approach consistent: Analyze each competitor using the same methods and depth so your comparisons stay reliable and your strategic insights stay balanced
 Customize your report: Adjust our competitive analysis template to meet your needs. For example, you might want to analyze competitors’ technology and infrastructure, culture and talent, and business partnerships, which our template doesn’t cover.
 Pair tools with thoughtful analysis: Competitive intelligence tools surface the data, but the patterns and nuances come from your own analysis. AI chatbots like ChatGPT can speed up your analysis.
A Semrush account gives you access to the tools you'll need throughout this process, including the Traffic & Market Toolkit for checking competitors’ traffic sources, and the AI Visibility Toolkit for finding AI visibility gaps.

Published in For Teams
How to create a competitive analysis: A beginner's guide
6 min read
Share this post
Making the hands-down best product in the market is an admirable goal, but it's often unrealistic.
No matter how much research you put into polishing your projects, competitors are always waiting, watching, and ready to pounce when they see an opportunity to one-up other companies — including yours. Leaders who ignore what their rivals are up to may wake up one morning to find their once-dominant market position on a steady decline.
Project managers should frequently run competitive analysis reports to prevent competitors from gaining ground and gobbling up more market share. Let’s explore the benefits of competitive market analysis and the basics of constructing an effective competitor analysis framework.
What’s competitive analysis?
Competitive analysis is a business tactic used to identify competing companies and evaluate their marketing techniques to generate ideas and strengthen your brand's position.
Teams often use spreadsheet templates to organize key data points on their competitors — including consumer personas, revenue, and location — and contrast this information with internal reports and industry-wide metrics. Companies typically leverage competitive analysis to gain a high-level view of multiple competitors, but they may also concentrate on a few significant rivals in more detailed reports.
A competitive analysis often arranges companies in one of three categories depending on their threat level:
 Direct — direct competitors are the easiest to identify since these businesses offer similar products or services and target your consumer base. For example, direct competitors to a café chain like Starbucks also offer handcrafted beverages — with a heavy emphasis on coffee — as well as light snacks and sweets (think Tim Hortons or Dunkin' Donuts).
 Indirect — indirect competitors sell or specialize in different products, but they operate in your company's business category and focus on the same audience. For instance, fast-food burger chains like McDonald's or Wendy's aren't associated with Starbucks' café niche, but they also offer ways for customers to quickly and conveniently pick up food and beverages.
 Replacement — also called "substitute" or "phantom" competitors, a replacement competitor is any business in a different product category that still offers a solution to a customer's primary problem. For example, if a gas station offers grab-and-go coffee and pastries, it gives Starbucks customers a competing option to satisfy their cravings for a caffeinated beverage and snack. Packaged coffee products in the grocery store could also be a substitute competitor to Starbucks' business model. Because the category is rather broad, companies often have the most challenging time identifying and quantifying the impact of replacement competitors.
Why conduct market competition analysis?
Conducting competitive analysis is far more than just “spying” on rival companies to figure out their secret recipe for success. The data from these analyses can help your business better understand its current market position and inform your strategies to achieve dominance in the upcoming quarters.
Here are a few more reasons you should consider running a competitive analysis:
 Identify strengths and weaknesses — some of the most influential findings from a competitor analysis appear after identifying and contrasting strengths and weaknesses between your company and its competitors. Knowing what's going right and wrong for others can help the team spot their most significant threats, advantages, and vulnerabilities.
 Generate ideas for new business tactics — the information you gather from a competitive analysis reveals business challenges and opportunities, which empower your team members to brainstorm effective marketing strategies that play to your strengths. A competitive analysis report also encourages you to see problems from a different perspective and determine the most pressing priorities.
 Establish measurable benchmarks — because competitive analysis is a comparison tool, it highlights your team's position relative to peers in terms of brand recognition, size, and market penetration. Knowing where other companies stand provides a benchmark to measure future growth and track the success of new initiatives.
 Visualize industry trends — after scanning multiple competitors, you may notice broad trends in your industry that reveal actionable information about consumer behavior or shifts in the marketing landscape. Whether your company opts to join a new trend or take a counter-approach is up to you, but recognizing these patterns is key to making informed operational and marketing decisions.
How to do a competitive analysis: A 5-step strategy
Without a coherent framework for recognizing worthwhile information, it's easy to feel overwhelmed during the data collection process.
Before scoping out competitors for details, ensure you have a clear system in place to make sense of all this information. We suggest this five-step strategy for competitive analysis:
1. Identify and classify competing companies
The first step in any competitive analysis is to determine key competitors and choose which ones to include in your study.
Although you may already have a shortlist of rivals you want to explore, see if any unexpected names pop up after a quick Google search for alternative brands. It's also helpful to review survey data from existing customers about companies they view as competitors and their opinions on these businesses.
Online forums, social media pages, and review sites may also contain noteworthy information about competitors worth adding to your analysis. For optimal diversity, try to include companies of various sizes and stages of development in the direct, indirect, and replacement categories.
2. Organize data in a competitor analysis template
After selecting the companies to include in your competitor analysis, it's time to arrange them in a grid alongside the major metrics you intend to review (such as average revenue, company size, and brand awareness).
Sometimes called a “competitor matrix,” these templates typically use spreadsheets or tables for clean organization and easy scannability. This format also encourages teams to keep their comments as concise and direct as possible, usually in bullet point format.
3. Gather information on competing companies
To avoid information overload, encourage team members to focus on the four Ps of marketing — product, price, promotion, and place — and make the most of their search time. These four elements give an overview of a competitor's core offerings, as well as the amount people pay for a product or service, standard marketing practices, and geographical penetration.
Start by reviewing a company's website, social media feeds, and press releases to find official data on the brand's identity and size. It can also be helpful to review sites like LinkedIn or Glassdoor to get a sense of the organization’s revenue and employee pool. And don’t forget to check out third-party review sites like TrustPilot to see unbiased opinions about the competitor's offerings.
4. Develop target customer personas
Once you have a clear picture of each competitor's history, market position, and primary offerings, develop customer personas and see whether there are any significant differences between them and your target audience.
Pay careful attention to the company's official mission statement, social media campaigns, and customer spotlights when imagining the consumers a competitor likely has in mind. These consumer insights can add clarity to customer campaigns and spark fresh ideas for distinguishing your product strategies from similar brands.
5. Perform a SWOT analysis
A SWOT analysis — short for strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats — can help your team make actionable use of the competitor data.
